description: The Cognitive Gauge (CogGauge) tool aims to develop a portable gaming application that assesses cognitive state of astronaut crew members with the goal of determining probable causes of observed cognitive deficits. CogGauge, while engaging astronauts in an entertaining experience, combines predictive tools for assessing cognitive workload with metrics that assess performance decrements. CogGauge uses a hybrid approach combining predictive workload values with behavioral/performance-based workload assessment across a number of task difficulty levels. This comprehensive approach takes into consideration learning effects across a number of cognitive tasks (i.e., mini-games in the gaming context) and derives assessment of performance decrements related to cognitive deficits to identify probable causes of cognitive decrement. Feedback from CogGauge may be provided to astronauts and/or flight surgeons to determine impact on space flight and missions. POTENTIAL NASA COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS: CogGauge, once developed, forms a foundation for several potential tools for use within NASA. For example, the underlying framework that utilizes a combination of predictive workload and performance/behavioral measures can be used to build several tools that could be integrated within shuttle (or its future replacements) controls to assess astronaut cognitive workload during a mission. Another possible expansion is to assess ground operations centers workload while monitoring a mission progress. In essence, the concepts/approach implemented in CogGauge could potentially expand to several applications within NASA that involve intense human-system integration.
research_impact: In terms of other government and commercial markets, CogGauge could be potentially tailored for use by aircraft pilots to assess their cognitive workload before/after long flying hours. In many situations, the approach/algorithms implemented in CogGauge could be used to model an operator interacting with a complex system, such as Command and Control, Power Plant Control Units, Nursing Stations, and so on. In today's net-centric work environment, operators are required to consume multiple streams of data simultaneously from several monitor stations, which can lead to issues of cognitive overload, decreased performance, and loss of situation awareness. CogGauge could be adapted to monitor operator workload in real-time and drive potential adaptations to displays/task demands to minimize times of overload. Such an extension of CogGauge may be useful in domains such as airport security checkpoints, customs, police stations, etc.

title: Modeling Phase Change and Thermocapillary Flow in the Constrained Vapor Bubble Experiment Reduce
pi_affiliation: Ajaev, Vladimir Ph.D. / Southern Methodist University

description: We propose theoretical and numerical studies of constrained vapor-liquid interfaces in the presence of phase change, i.e., evaporation and/or condensation. These studies will result in better understanding of heat and mass transfer in two-phase systems in which the effects of capillary forces and thermocapillarity are important. The main focus of the work is on a specific geometric configuration used in a recent space experiment, referred to as a Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB). We propose to use asymptotic methods to simplify the system of governing equations for fluid flow and heat transfer for this configuration, followed by numerical solutions of the resulting equations using modern computational techniques. The proposed work has a wide range of ground and space applications including two-phase cooling systems for traditional electronic devices such as laptop computers as well as novel thermal management systems for emerging applications such as proton exchange membrane fuel cells and photovoltaic cells for solar energy harvesting. The small length scales in many of these systems imply that interfacial phenomena are very important while the effects of gravity are secondary. Some aspects of the proposed work are also relevant for modeling of physical processes such as self-assembly of colloidal particles from evaporating droplets, condensation of droplets in novel devices for energy conversion, and water desalination. The liquid transport mechanisms by capillary forces are also important to study for space applications, such as advanced cooling systems for spacecraft, since conventional methods for liquid transport can fail or become impractical in such applications. For example, any system that relies on the force of gravity for functioning is likely to fail in the microgravity environment. Transporting liquids by external pressure gradients, while not impossible in space, typically requires mechanical pumps, often making such systems impractical because of the payload weight restrictions.
research_impact: The proposed work has a wide range of ground and space applications. These include two-phase cooling systems for traditional electronic devices, such as laptop computers, as well as novel thermal management systems for emerging applications, such as proton exchange membrane fuel cells and photovoltaic cells for solar energy harvesting.
task_progress: FINAL REPORTING OCTOBER 2021 The Principal Investigator (Dr. Ajaev) at Southern Methodist University and his graduate student conducted detailed studies of heat transfer and fluid flow in the wedge-flow geometry with parameters corresponding to the Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) experiment. Liquid flow velocity and vapor-liquid interface temperatures were determined from the model, resulting in new physical insight into the nature of transport phenomena in the CVB and estimation of the significance of Marangoni stresses. Different values of the heat transfer coefficients are predicted in different parts of the CVB system. The significance of inertia effects in both liquid and gas flow is discussed in connection with formation of the pinch points at the interfaces and central droplets observed in experiments under the conditions of microgravity. Shapes of the central droplets formed away from the two ends of the CVB cuvette have been determined by the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) team from the experimental data, followed by development of novel mathematical models of evaporating/condensing sessile droplets. The models were implemented based on several in-house codes and new subroutines accounting for previously neglected physical effects. In particular, both perfect wetting and partial wetting regimes can be studied by adjusting the non-dimensional parameters in the code. By incorporating the heat conduction in the substrate under the droplet, agreement between theory and experimental data from J. Plawsky’s group (RPI) was obtained. Increase in the contact angle and effects of the heat conduction in the wall are shown to result in reduction of phase change rates near the contact line. Substantial work on data analysis was also conducted at RPI leading to new results on the effect of condenser temperature on the interface shapes. The effect of heater power on the pressure in the system was investigated, leading to identification of three different linear regimes with different slopes. Linear correlation between the location of the central droplet and surface tension gradient is found. The RPI team also conducted new ground-based experiments to study adsorbed films on the walls of the cuvette for different liquids and carried out phase-field numerical simulations to determine liquid-vapor interface shapes for constrained vapor bubbles in rectangular cuvette. title: Cell:Cell Mediated Assembly of Cardiac Tissue in Microgravity Environments Reduce
discipline_element: Physical Sciences : BIOTECHNOLOGY--Cellular biotechnology & tissue engineering

pi_address: Department of Biomedical Research P.O. Box 269 Wilmington , DE 19899
description: This project addresses aspects of cardiac tissue engineering. The capacity of isolated rat and human heart cells to reconstitute cardiac tissue in culture without extensive cues from three-dimensional scaffolds or matrices is being investigated. The approach takes full advantage of the simulated-microgravity environment provided by NASA-bioreactors to allow isolated cells to re-establish tissue structure in vitro. The proposed research also investigates the role of gravity and the bioreactor environment in the structural and molecular/biochemical phenotype of cardiac cell assemblages. A combination of morphological, cell biological, molecular, and biochemical methods will be used to characterize cardiac cell cultures and to compare bioreactor-derived cultures to native tissue and to cultures grown using standard tissue culture methods. In the long-term, it is hoped that this study will lead to the ability to engineer biosynthetic cardiac patches for the treatment of a wide variety of cardiac abnormalities. Further, it is hoped that this research will lead to an increased understanding of the influence of gravity on cells and cell assemblages in culture. The work investigates the ability of isolated heart cells to re-establish structural and molecular/biochemical phenotypes of heart tissue when cultured in microgravity environments. In particular, the study will: 1)Evaluate the process by which cardiac-specific structures are formed by isolated rat and human cardiac cells. 2)Identity the extra-cellular matrix (ECM) material that is differentially produced in bioreactor-based cultures. 3) Assess the role of gravity in determining the distribution of subcellular organelles in cultured heart cells. 4) Evaluate the effect of bioreactor-based culture on signal transduction pathways. 5)Determine the changes in gene expression caused by culture in microgravity using differential display RT-PCR. For Spaceflight: The long-term presence of humans in space will require that critical medical and surgical procedures be conducted at remote sites utilizing limited resources. Of particular concern will be the ability to maintain adequate circulatory function, which is required to sustain life and to allow crew-members to remain productive during flight and thereafter. Among the issues of relevance to NASA's spaceflight programs, two are critical. First, physical and pharmacologic countermeasures that allow crew members to remain productive during shifting hemodynamic-loading conditions associated with changes in gravity are needed; strategies that require limited additional "upweight" would be especially useful. Our studies focus on pathways that impact the organization and function of cardiac muscle in order to develop pharmacologic interventions that will improve circulatory function under changing conditions or in disease. We have identified a number of potentialyy importnat pathways including a heme-metabolic pathway that may be amenable to pharmacologic manipulations using simple and naturally-occurring compounds. Stimulation of this pathway improves cardiac muscle cell organization and function. Second, there is a need to develop strategies that reverse or repair profound heart disease that may arise in crew members. Heart disease, which is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in humans, may occur as a direct result of the spaceflight environment, as a secondary result of accommodation to long-term mission conditions, or as a consequence of unanticipated disease, injury, or infection. Our studies are directed toward the development of implantable constructs produced on site using defined media with primary isolated cells and simple bioreactors. Thus, although at an early stage, our research may be highly relevant to the development of strategies supporting the long-term presence of humans in space. On Earth: Congenital and acquired heart diseases are significant problems. The treatments that are currently available mainly address the sequelae of primary defects and often fall short of full structural and functional recovery. In addition, there is a severe shortage of donor tissue for reconstructive cardiac surgery and transplantation. Advances in treatment are hampered by a lack of suitable material and a lack of characterization of the molecular pathways that establish and sustain tissue structure. New treatments for heart diseases, new sources of implant materials, and accessible models for the study of cardiac morphogenetic pathways are all needed, and tissue-engineering has emerged as a potential means to address these areas. Cardiac tissue engineering is an emerging field involving the construction of tissue equivalents in vitro. Using an approach in which self-assembly is encouraged, work by the applicant shows that isolated neonatal rat heart cells (NRHCs) re-establish characteristics of three-dimensional cardiac tissue when grown in specialized bioreactors. Through the use of NASA biotechnologies, our knowledge of the mechanisms and pathways involved with in vitro tissuegenesis is being extended so that an accessible source of tissue-equivalent material can be developed. The development of tissue-equivalents for use as research models or for use as implant devices could profoundly alter the course of cardiac-related research and dramatically improve the outlook for patients with a variety of heart diseases.
task_progress: Results during the 3.5 years of study funded by NAG9-1339 establish a framework for the mechanistic understanding of de novo cardiac tissuegenesis and of the role of heme metabolic pathways in modulating cardiac muscle phenotype. Crucial steps have been taken toward developing strategies to manipulate cardiac cells, to improve cardiac performance, and to repair damaged cardiac tissue. Further studies are needed to understand the behavior of cardiac cells and cardiac stem cells in microgravity environments, to probe the mechanisms by which heme oxygenase-mediated pathways improve cardiac organization and function while protecting against oxidative injury, and to assess the application of these emerging therapeutic strategies in models of heart disease. This work represents the initial phase in the development of advanced counter-measures to enhance cardiac performance and to repair damaged cardiac tissue using approaches that are suitable for long-term NASA missions.

description: We are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe. An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow us to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Our proposed ground-based investigations with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.
research_impact: An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in medical MRI. As a result, at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system). The recent progress made in our lab lays the foundation for the continued development of hyperpolarized xenon MRI for brain imaging. Specifically, imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis) and angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system), are now viable research goals. Because HP 129Xe is an MR signal source with properties very different from those generated from water-protons, it may yield structural and functional information not detectable by proton-based MRI methods. Thus brain imaging with hyperpolarized xenon should be of great benefit to the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of a number of neurological diseases.

task_progress: [Ed. note 3/23/2012: compiled from Final Report submitted to JSC Human Research Program in July 2011 and received by Task Book February 2012] In work by the PI and others, HP noble gas MRI using 3He and 129Xe has been established to provide highly detailed images of the lungs and brain, and offers the immense advantage of providing information on physiological function, including lung ventilation (3He or 129Xe), lung perfusion (129Xe), and cerebral blood flow (129Xe). For example, HP gas MRI allows investigators to pinpoint precise sections of the lungs where gas is reaching, and where gas is not reaching (ventilation defects), something other measurements of lung function cannot do. Because of its greater sensitivity, HP gas MRI can detect pulmonary or cerebral dysfunction at earlier stages, allowing treatment or counteracting measures to be provided earlier and with greater effectiveness. In addition, HP gas MRI provides imaging of physiological function without exposing subjects to ionizing radiation or chemical contrast agents. This increases safety, and also allows investigators and/or care providers to non-invasively image subjects repeatedly over time. In this study, our specific research accomplishments included the following: Extending the Frequency of the 1.5 T Signa MRI Scanner to 3He Human Lung Imaging Using HP 3He Development of Imaging Pulse Sequences for HP Gas MRI Small Airway Imaging of the Human Lungs Human 3D Airway Tree Rendering Dynamically Adaptive MRI Optical-Flow Imaging of Rat Lung Dynamics HP 129Xe Lifetimes (T1) in Blood Temporal Dynamics of 129Xe in Living Rats Cerebral Perfusion Measurement Using HP 129Xe

task_progress: The overall goal of this proposal is to develop hyperpolarized noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (HP MRI) for the assessment of pulmonary and nervous system damage that may be incurred during human space flight. Hyperpolarized noble gas MRI is showing dramatic results for diagnostic imaging of the lungs, brain, and other parts of the body, some of which have been resistant to conventional proton MRI. Most notably, we have achieved highresolution dynamic images of the lungs and airways using hyperpolarized 3He, and have measured cerebral perfusion and functional activity in the brain using hyperpolarized 129Xe (HP 129Xe). The number of space flight-related pathologies which may benefit from this technique are vast and range from pulmonary dysfunction caused by microgravity to cognitive and neurobehavioral problems resulting from the stress and isolation of extended term space travel. This novel technology should also offer a rapid, sensitive method to detect treatment effects and thus may expedite the development of therapeutic strategies for treating space flight related injury, such as aerosol administration of drugs via the lungs, which may obviate the need for medicinal injections during space flight. description: A novel biomedical imaging technique, hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is capable of generating high-resolution images of the lung, heart, and brain by using the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe. The HP gases, created via spin-exchange optical pumping, have greatly enhanced MR detectability. Unlike conventional proton MRI, HP gas MRI does not require a large magnetic field and, therefore, can be performed in very low magnetic fields (~ 0.01 Tesla). Thus, a small, portable, low-power MRI system, practical for space-flight, may be designed to implement very low field HP gas MRI. The imaging capacity of HP gas MRI itself is also relevant to space flight research. research_impact: Today, more than ever, the understanding of pulmonary function has become critical to the treatment of disease and to the health of the community at large. The economic cost of pulmonary disease is estimated to be over ten billion dollars a year. The personal cost, although not quantifiable, is no doubt enormous. task_progress: [Ed. note 3/23/2012: compiled from Final Report submitted to JSC Human Research Program in July 2011 and received by Task Book February 2012] Hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas MRI using 3He or 129Xe provides highly detailed images of the lungs and brain, and offers the immense advantage of providing information on physiological function, including lung ventilation (3He or 129Xe), lung perfusion (129Xe), and cerebral blood flow (129Xe). For example, HP gas MRI allows investigators to pinpoint precise sections of the lungs where gas is reaching, and where gas is not reaching (ventilation defects), something other measurements of lung function cannot do. Because of its greater sensitivity, HP gas MRI can detect pulmonary or cerebral dysfunction at earlier stages, allowing treatment or counteracting measures to be provided earlier and with greater effectiveness. In addition, HP gas MRI provides imaging of physiological function without exposing subjects to ionizing radiation or chemical contrast agents. This increases safety, and also allows investigators and/or care providers to non-invasively image subjects repeatedly over time. HP gas MRI has countless applications to evaluating vascular and pulmonary problems that could arise in human space flight. Such applications include investigating the effects of microgravity and pressure changes on the physiological functioning of the lungs, and studying the effects of microgravity and pressure changes associated with space flight on vascular functioning. In addition, HP gas MRI is ideal for evaluating aerosol drug administration, a delivery method of particular interest for space flight because it avoids the need for injections of medicines in space. In this study, we further developed hyperpolarized noble gas MRI for use in examining pulmonary and brain function in animal models and in humans, building upon previous work by the PI funded by NASA. HP gas MRI has immense potential for applications to the study of the physiology of the lungs and brain, and for helping diagnose and inform treatment for adverse reactions to microgravity and low pressure environments. Low-magnetic-field MRI, which is made possible by HP gas MRI, is particularly advantageous in this regard because it provides extraordinarily detailed images of lung and brain function with lightweight, low-cost, easy-to-operate equipment that could be used in space environments. With the assistance of generous funding from NASA, our group was able to make significant advances in many areas of HP gas MRI, including pulmonary ventilation analysis and low-magnetic-field MRI. In this study, our specific research accomplishments included the following: Ventilation Heterogeneity of Asthma Evaluated Using Hyperpolarized 3He MRI Functional Imaging of the Brain Using Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI Using Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI to Image Stroke Hyperpolarized 3He MRI Evaluation of Radiation Therapy for Non-small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) Assessment of Ventilation Function and Airway Structure in Mesothelioma Using Hyperpolarized 3He MRI Resolving the Conflict of Hyperpolarized 129Xe T1 Values in the Rat Brain Very Low field Lung MRI using Hyperpolarized 3He Developing small, distal airway imaging to resolutions below 1mm

task_progress: Experiments are ongoing for imaging the ventilation and airways of asthmatic and non-asthmatic subjects with HP 3He MRI. With simultaneous lung mechanics measurements, lung ventilation are being mapped and compared between the two subject populations, and the associated airway structure are being correlated with lung mechanical properties. In addition to our lung studies, advances have been made in our effort to develop hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI for the assessment of brain structure and function. The three most significant advances in this area include: 1. The method of chemical shift imaging was validated in our laboratory. 2. Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI CSI was carried out in rat brain. 3. In vivo Functional Brain Imaging Using Hyperpolarized 129 Xe was demonstrated. Previously, we reported that the rigorous airway diameter quantification algorithm we developed has been tested on an anthropomorphic lung phantom, and presented the results. In the past year, 5 subjects who have had their airways scanned using HP 3He MRI have also been imaged with CT. The algorithm computing the local ventilation coefficient of variation from HP 3He MR images previously developed was applied to all ventilation data sets available. The resulting heterogeneity maps, viewed in the context of the ventilation maps, clearly demonstrate the capture of the ventilation heterogeneity characteristics. The algorithms for mapping ventilation have been applied to 4 non-asthmatics and 13 asthmatic subjects. Statistical significant differences were observed in the heterogeneity scores as well as ventilation distribution standard deviation for various cases of comparison. The results of this study support the idea that HP 3He MRI can serve as a diagnostic tool that can be regularly used to evaluate astronaut physiology, how that differs from their earth status, how it progresses with continued space flight, and how it alters in the presence of disease or impairment. description: We are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe. An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow us to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Our proposed ground-based investigations with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.
research_impact: An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in medical MRI. As a result, at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system).
task_progress: Adjustment of the TR (repeat time) parameter on the scans has been discovered to enable decreasing the static ventilation scan time from 10-13 seconds, down to 5-8 seconds. This gain cuts down on the time subjects need to hold their breath, which can be very helpful for patients with pulmonary diseases, vastly reducing their discomfort. A model-based approach has been developed to measure the diameters of airways captured with the dynamic imaging protocols. The rigor of this approach virtually eliminates the dependence on the unreliable human detection of airway edges, and the resultant randomness by which diameter endpoints are selected.

description: The in-flight video recording capabilities planned for the Bion-M1 Project make possible a new generation of science on unmanned satellites. The present proposal is to analyze rodent behavior across the one-month duration of the orbital flight of Bion-M1. The specific, testable hypotheses for Bion-M1 include microgravity effects on the kinds and amounts of behavior that rodents will express. General activity and its circadian pattern will be examined, and specific functional categories of individual and group social behaviors will be characterized and quantified. Kinematic measures of limb and trunk movements will also be taken. Modification of individual and group behavior can alter immune, endocrine, and physiological function. By integrating behavioral data with those from the same animals studied by various primary and secondary study PIs, it will be possible to test alternative explanations for alterations in immune, musculoskeletal, neural, and endocrine changes with spaceflight.
research_impact: The planned scientific studies for Bion M-1 are primarily in the realm of basic, "fundamental biology," but the studies will be pioneering in many ways and are capable of spawning exciting Earth benefits, mostly in the realm of insights into fundamental biological processes related to immune function, muscle and bone integrity, and adaptation of the nervous system.
task_progress: [Ed. note: compiled in July 2019 from PI final report submitted to the NASA Shared Services Center in November 2015 ; received in July 2019 by NASA Ames and then to Task Book] The Bion M-1 mission presented an exciting opportunity for studying adult mice during a relatively long-duration (one month) exposure to spaceflight conditions and immediately upon recovery on Earth. The design of this Russian flight experiment was based on group-housed male mice (three adult male, C57/Bl6 mice per compartment). Some of the mice were equipped with implanted telemetry equipment that provided heart rate and blood pressure data. Significantly for the present report, the Bion compartments provided on-board video surveillance of the mice, with significant volume of daily storage. Upon landing, the present effort included post-flight behavioral testing of the mice. Conventional wisdom has long held that unrelated adult male mice cannot be housed together without competition over resources such as space and access to resources, pathological stress, and fighting. NASA has incorporated such concerns into their life sciences operations, thus limiting the use of this valuable mammalian model for flight-based investigations. Bion M-1 procedures and results contributed an important alteration to the conventional wisdom, and the video data and direct observations that comprised the present investigations provide valuable information. We learned that the Russian scientists employed several innovative, yet simple techniques to produce triads of unrelated adult male mice that lived amicably in the small housing compartments for one month. This was accomplished by establishing, in their laboratory vivarium, triads of adult males. They were housed in a standard cage and provided a shelter apparatus to share. Mice that did not share the shelter were thus screen and eliminated from the pool. There followed a regime of daily handling. These animals were also maintained at about 90% ad lib body weight for purposes of operant training. These procedures yielded groups of adult males that lived together amicably in the Bion habitats in microgravity and under Earth-based control conditions. Their excellent performance violated the conventional wisdom and provides an important example of how we might well use group-housed male mice in future studies.

description: Microgravity and Ground-based experimental studies of premixed-flame propagation in low-intensity turbulent flow under microgravity conditions are to be undertaken The focus of the research is on the hydrodynamic coupling between flame and flow-field dynamics at low turbulence intensities, which may lead to flame-generated turbulence, flame acceleration and enhancement of burning rates. As a result of hydrodynamic coupling the transition from initially planar or wrinkled laminar flames to fast turbulent flames or detonations is possible, even when diffusive-thermal effects associated with non-unity reactant Lewis numbers are not destabilizing. Therefore, the proposed work is relevant to microgravity fire safety.
task_progress: During the past year, we have completed construction of a new non-rotating burner to be used for ground-based and microgravity studies of the Darrieus-Landau hydrodynamic instability on annular-flame propagation. We have also developed and tested new optical tools to enable measurements of turbulence properties in a second, rotating burner to be under construction soon. Preliminary ground-based studies will be carried out at UC Davis over the next few months, after-which microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn Research Center will be conducted.

description: NCSER is a non-profit organization, created in 1997 as the National Center for Microgravity Research under the sponsorship of NASA through a cooperative agreement with Universities Space Research Association (USRA) and Case Western Reserve University. The NCSER is physically located on the campus of CWRU and at NASA GRC where NCSER scientists and engineers are work together with GRC personnel. The role of the NCSER is to • Perform research in fluids and combustion to support NASA’s space program and related national initiatives • Increase awareness of microgravity research and enhance its scientific, technological, educational, and economic impacts • Support the development of enabling technologies for space exploration Originally chartered with supporting and developing NASA microgravity experiments on the ‘shuttle’ and ISS, the combined NCSER expertise in fluids and combustion processes in reduced gravity (i.e., microgravity, Lunar and Martian gravity) is second to none. Our current in-house expertise includes fluids management and control in reduced gravity, reduced gravity combustion processes; microfluidics, heat transfer and phase change processes; computational multiphase fluid dynamics and heat and mass transfer, computational simulation of biomedical processes in support of the ‘Digital Astronaut’ for autonomous space medicine. NCSER scientists and engineers are currently engaged in long term research related to NASA’s exploration vision: Current investigations include: fire safety- flammability, suppression and detection, propellant management, and fluids processes for advanced human support technologies.
task_progress: NCSER was formed in February 2005, evolving from the former National Center for Microgravity Research (NCMR) in response to NASA’s new research focus in its Vision for Space Exploration (VSE) and in order to better address topics of relevance. The NCMR was originally chartered with supporting NASA’s microgravity research programs in fluids and combustion and facilitated fluids and combustion research by assembling a cadre of in-house subject matter expertise in these areas, and by serving as Technical Monitors for grants, Project Scientists, and project support staff for flight experiments. From 1997 to 2007, NCSER staff members were Principal Investigators (PIs) and Co-investigators (Co-Is) on numerous competitively awarded grants. An independent review panel convened by Dr. Eugene Trinh, then Chief of NASA’s microgravity science division in 2002, stated that “NCMR is a vital and successful operation, effectively supporting NASA’s program in many ways” and encouraged NASA to “regard NCMR as a kind of small-scale laboratory of innovative research management”. Dr. Trinh concluded, “The Center has performed with distinction in its core responsibilities of supporting NASA’s research programs in fluids and combustion”. More recently, as NASA has risen to the challenge of adjusting to its new role in space exploration, NCSER scientists and engineers have responded by successfully shifting focus and transitioning from activities conducted under NASA’s former microgravity research program to critically new research and technology development relevant to space exploration. The flexibility and responsiveness demonstrated in this transition is due to the breadth of science and engineering disciplines resident within NSCER and their relevance to exploration systems technology developments at GRC and other NASA centers. Indeed, NCSER’s past experience with the effects of the space environment, especially reduced gravity effects on multiphase fluid and reacting flow processes associated with exploration systems and technologies, is directly applicable to ongoing and anticipated exploration research and technology development and for defining and/or designing methods to mitigate the negative effects of the space environment. During the period 2006-2008 amid NASA’s restructuring of their programs at Glenn Research Center, the NCSER underwent a change in focus, moving away from a large role in supporting ISS microgravity research and toward research motivated by space exploration technology needs and challenges.. In particular, our staff scientists were able to apply their expertise in reduced-gravity fluids, combustion and reacting flow processes to research related to spacecraft thermal and fluid systems, fire safety and astronaut health. The NCSER focused around five activities during the period 2006-2008: • Exploration Systems Technology Research • Engineering Research Support • ISS Research and Pl support • Workshop and Conference Organization and Support Because of its core competencies in the physical/chemical sciences and expertise in low-gravity fluids transport, combustion and reacting flow phenomena, the NCSER has established partnerships to deal with a broad spectrum of problems related to the development of enabling technologies for space exploration. These problems range from thermal control, water management and waste processing in life support systems, to fire safety, to multiphase fluid management in power and propulsion, in-situ resource utilization and on to bioscience and medical technologies and counter-measures. NCSER was operated through Cooperative Agreement NCC3-975 that continued through June 30th, 2008. The NCSER is a collaborative arrangement between the Universities Space Research Association (USRA), Case Western Reserve University and NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). It combines the breadth and depth of USRA’s nationally distributed organization with two of Northeast Ohio’s research powerhouses to produce a potent combination of skills and expertise in reduced gravity fluids and combustion research that is applied to problems of significance. Thus, NCSER provides research avenues that, by filling gaps in knowledge, will lead to an important foundation upon which broadly applicable new technologies can be developed for use in future systems developed by various NASA Enterprises.

title: Vibrations and g-Jitter: Transport Disturbances Due to Residual Acceleration During Low Gravity Directional Solidification Experiments Reduce
pi_affiliation: Alexander, J. Iwan D. Ph.D. / Case Western Reserve University
pi_address: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering 305 Olin, 10900 Euclid Avenue Cleveland , OH 44106
description: The experimental objectives are to characterize the response of heat and species transport in a directionally solidifying model transparent alloy system subject to well-characterized imposed vibrations and ultimately to spacecraft residual acceleration. The temperature and composition fields will be measured using two-color holographic interferometry to characterize the composition and temperature fields simultaneously. The convective flows will be visualized using a shadowgraph technique and selected experiments will involve Particle Image Velocimetry. These experiments will be accompanied by numerical modeling that will be used extend the ground-based experimental results and to assist in the definition of a set of benchmark flight experiments. The experiments will: · Quantify the effects of residual acceleration on transport in compositionally inhomogeneous liquids and on transport during directional solidification. · Investigate vibrational convective transport under 1 g conditions in transparent model systems (succinonitrile-water, SCN-W) using High and low frequency translational vibrations and Rotational vibrations. · Investigate single and two-liquid phase melt responses. · Compare thermosolutal and dominantly thermal convective responses to vibration (facilitated by the weak dependence of SCN-W density on composition). · Investigate the possibility of using vibration for transport control (e.g., for melt homogenization or rehomogenization). The objective is to characterize the response of heat and species during directional solidification of a binary alloy system subject to translational and rotational vibration. This will be accomplished through a combination of ground-based experiments and numerical simulation. The work will lead to the definition of benchmark flight experiments that will unambiguously characterize the response of solidification systems to spacecraft residual acceleration in low-earth orbit. Since the ground-based work involves vibrations that either correspond to modulations of 1 g or are lateral vibrations in the presence of steady 1 g acceleration, the emphasis of the ground-based work will be on the generation of mean flows at higher frequencies. The design of experiment facilities and planning of specific experiments for the International Space Station and other orbital platforms requires that the experiment’s sensitivity to microgravity residual acceleration be assessed. Residual acceleration arises due to transient and vibrational disturbances (g-jitter), atmospheric drag on the spacecraft, and the gravity gradient. The interaction of residual acceleration with density gradients in fluids will generally produce buoyancy driven flows within those fluids. Experiments involving fluids with density gradients are conducted in low gravity so that buoyant convective motion that is unavoidable under terrestrial conditions is reduced or eliminated. To make best use of the available experiment time and to eliminate any ambiguities in the interpretation of experiment results it is therefore essential to assess the sensitivity of a given experiment to time-dependent and steady acceleration. To date, nearly all the work that addresses the impact of residual acceleration on low-gravity experiments relies on the results of numerical modeling and scaling analyses. Experimental quantification or verification is all but lacking. On the other hand, questions regarding the possible influence of residual acceleration effects on actual flight experiments still persist. The recent MEPHISTO flight experiments (conducted on USMP-3, in February-March 1996) were the first experiments to be conducted to characterize the effects of impulse disturbances (caused by thruster firings) on transport during directional solidification. The experiment results clearly demonstrated the ability of numerical models to predict the convective transport response to impulse disturbances. However, a quantitative characterization of experiment response to other forms of g-jitter acceleration is still lacking, most notably in the area of vibration and rotational acceleration. (Note that for rotational accelerations that involve “pendulum” or rocking type motions, fluid motion can occur even in the absence of density gradients). Without quantitative experimental verification, model predictions of experiment response to g-jitter are of limited use and could lead to unnecessary design restrictions or unsuitable experiment operating conditions. Thus, to further improve our ability to predict the impact of vibration and rotational g-jitter acceleration, quantitative experimental data is needed. This will establish a set of benchmark results that can be used to unambiguously define the response of a well-characterized solidification experiment to residual acceleration.

description: Anecdotal and empirical findings collected in space and other extreme environments continue to highlight the potential for psychological symptoms and conditions to degrade crew performance, increase conflict, and jeopardize mission success. Indeed, ‘negative reactions’ during periods of isolation, confinement, demanding work schedules, stimulus reduction, separation from loved ones, sleep deprivation, and a host of other stressors are more appropriately viewed as normative rather than pathogenic. Selection methods and countermeasures serve to mitigate some degree of psychological risk, but long-duration space flight will substantially extend exposure to these and other stressors. Previous research documenting psychological symptoms experienced during space flight and in other isolated and confined environments (ICE) provides evidence of a wide range of psychological and behavioral reactions. Unfortunately however, these collective data ultimately serve to raise more questions than answers. Differences in collection methods, types of symptoms/reactions assessed, psychological constructs examined, and timing and duration of measurements limit conclusions that can be drawn from this research. As a result, understanding of the discrete symptoms and conditions most likely to occur during space flight and thus, ability to quantify the magnitude, probability, or consequences of such risk remains inadequate. The current project proposes to address these notable gaps in knowledge via three specific Aims. First, we will conduct extensive scientific literature reviews and interviews with subject matter experts in order to synthesize existing knowledge of the psychological and behavioral symptoms experienced in space and other extreme environments (Aim 1). Our review will directly inform the development of a comprehensive checklist of symptoms to be monitored among 6 separate cohorts (i.e., 2 Antarctic and 4 Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) cohorts)) as part of a longitudinal investigation (Aim 2). Symptoms will be examined based on their point/period prevalence, severity, and duration. The checklist will also be administered (repeatedly) in conjunction with a physical symptoms checklist in order to examine concurrent and sequential overlap between psychological and physical health symptoms as means of clarifying potential etiologies. Finally, our study will extend previous research by exploring relationships among psychological health, sleep loss/dysregulation, biomarkers of stress, and performance-based outcomes (Aim 3). A comprehensive battery of cognitive and performance measures (including a perception-action coupling task) will be administered repeatedly as part of our longitudinal study. These outcomes will inform a final list of psychological/ behavioral symptoms to be examined during an extended International Space Station (ISS) mission.
research_impact: Anecdotal and empirical findings collected in space and other extreme environments continue to highlight the potential for psychological symptoms and conditions to degrade crew performance, increase conflict, and jeopardize mission success. Indeed, ‘negative reactions’ during periods of isolation, confinement, demanding work schedules, stimulus reduction, separation from loved ones, sleep deprivation, and a host of other stressors are more appropriately viewed as normative rather than pathogenic. Selection methods and countermeasures serve to mitigate some degree of psychological risk, but long-duration space flight will substantially extend exposure to these and other stressors. Previous research documenting psychological symptoms experienced during space flight and in other isolated and confined environments (ICE) provides evidence of a wide range of psychological and behavioral reactions. Unfortunately however, these collective data ultimately serve to raise more questions than answers. Differences in collection methods, types of symptoms/reactions assessed, psychological constructs examined, and timing and duration of measurements limit conclusions that can be drawn from this research. As a result, understanding of the discrete symptoms and conditions most likely to occur during space flight and thus, ability to quantify the magnitude, probability, or consequences of such risk remains inadequate. Thus, there is a need to: (1) identify the psychological/behavioral symptoms that pose the greatest threat to performance; (2) provide accurate and acceptable risk thresholds; (3) inform screening and selection processes; (4) guide further development of suitable working practices (standard operating procedures); and (5) develop interventions and counter measures to mitigate these risks. This project specifically addresses several knowledge gaps related to Risks of Adverse Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders [Ed. note: August 2021--Gaps have changed since this grant was awarded in FY2015; see Human Research Roadmap https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/ ] including: Gap 1 (Need to identify and quantify the key threats to and promoters of mission relevant behavioral health and performance during exploration class missions) and Gap 3 (Need to identify and validate measures to monitor behavioral health and performance and determine acceptable thresholds for these measures during exploration missions). Our primary goal is to identify the psychological and behavioral health symptoms with the greatest likelihood of occurrence during extended human space flight/habitation to space and to estimate associated levels of threat imposed to mission-based performance. As a final deliverable, a checklist of symptoms will be developed for implementation during an ISS mission (>6 months) in order to determine its feasibility, reliability, and facilitation of evidence-based decision making with regard to crew health, safety, and mission success. As a first step, we will conduct extensive scientific literature reviews and interviews with subject matter experts in order to synthesize existing knowledge of the psychological and behavioral symptoms experienced in space and other extreme environments (Aim 1). Our review will directly inform the development of a comprehensive checklist of symptoms to be monitored in two longitudinal studies including one HERA campaign and cohorts at the McMurdo and South Pole Antarctic stations (Aim 2). The checklist will also be administered (repeatedly) in conjunction with a list of physical complaints in order to examine concurrent and sequential overlap between psychological and physical health symptoms. Finally, our study will extend previous research by exploring relationships among psychological health, sleep dysregulation, biomarkers of stress, and performance-based cognitive outcomes (Aim 3). A comprehensive battery of cognitive and performance measures will be administered in conjunction with our other measures as part of our longitudinal study. Outcomes will inform a final mental health checklist for use during long duration space flight. As a supplemental Aim, we will examine the reliability of our mental health checklist in two Antarctic cohorts at the Palmer station.
task_progress: All project Aims have been met. We developed a 23-item self-report Mental Health Checklist (MHCL) to assess psychological health in isolated confined extreme (ICE) settings. The MHCL includes three reliable subscales—positive adaptation, poor self-regulation, and anxious apprehension—each assessing unique aspects of psychological health. In a 9-month longitudinal study, we assessed 110 personnel stationed at either McMurdo (coastal station) or South Pole (inland station). At the South Pole station, a total of 22 participants were enrolled and 88 participants were enrolled at the McMurdo station. Because crew at McMurdo are not required to be on station for the entire winter season, there was variability in the number of monthly sessions completed at this station. Antarctic participants were predominantly White (94.5%, n = 104) males (80%, n = 88) between the ages of 22 and 70 years old (M = 37.63, SD = 11.95). Because the greatest number of McMurdo participants completed 6 months of assessments, this time point was used to compare monthly outcomes across the two stations. For all participants, MHCL positive adaptation scores decreased significantly and MHCL poor self-regulation scores increased significantly from baseline to the end of study. Overall change in MHCL anxious apprehension scores across mission were non-significant, though month-to-month variability was observed. Higher poor self-regulation scores were observed at McMurdo compared to the South Pole during the early months of the mission. Anxious apprehension scores were significantly higher at the McMurdo station than at South Pole during all months. Prevalence and severity of physical symptoms increased significantly from baseline to the end of study in the full Antarctic sample but there were no significant differences in physical symptoms between the two stations. Changes in biomarkers of stress (cortisol, DHEA, or the cortisol:DHEA ratios) were not observed from baseline to the end of the mission. However, cortisol and cortisol:DHEA ratios were significantly higher among McMurdo compared to South Pole participants. Cognitive performance was also examined monthly using the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), the Spaceflight Cognitive Assessment Tool for Windows (WinSCAT), and the Perception-Action Coupling Task (PACT). Performance on the WinSCAT improved during early mission months and was sustained through the end of the study. PACT performance decreased across mission, but no changes were observed in PVT scores. Several study participants underwent emergency evacuation from the McMurdo station during the study. We examined monthly reports, biomarkers, and cognitive performance among 4 evacuees compared to the remaining McMurdo sample (n = 84) to identify potential indicators of distress prior to evacuation. Emergency evacuation occurred for medical reasons (n = 2) or for psychiatric reasons (n = 2). Elevated MHCL anxious apprehension scores were most common among all evacuees. Elevated physical symptoms were also apparent in one psychiatric and one medical evacuee in the months prior to evacuation. We did not find any biomarker of stress or objective sleep regularity to differ among evacuees compared to the full sample. At the Palmer station, the MHCL measure was administered to 26 participants during two winter-over seasons. MHCL data were collected for 4 consecutive months. The Palmer station is similar to the McMurdo station in climate and its coastal location, but similar to the South Pole in terms of size/number of residents. Similar to Antarctic participants at the McMurdo and South Pole stations, positive adaptation scores declined across mission whereas changes in poor self-regulation were more modest. The greatest increases in anxious apprehension scores were observed in later mission months. Collective findings indicate the MHCL is a reliable and useful measure for assessing psychological risk in ICE settings. Each of the MHCL scales contributes unique information in this regard, particularly when combined with assessment of physical complaints.

description: The objective of this research is to study the effect of gravity on the cytoplasmic and chloroplastic calcium profile in aequorin-transfomed Moss, Physcomitrella patens, using bioluminescence measurement with genetic reporter. This multi-disciplinary research program will focus on understanding the effect of gravity on calcium release in cytoplasm and chloroplast using photonic spectroscopy technology and transgenic techniques. The main effects to be studied are 1) the role of gravistimulation on the change in calcium release by in situ measurement of bioluminescence from moss expressing apoaequorin mounted on a traditional clinostat, 2) investigate, in situ, the change in the dynamics of cytoplasmic and chloroplastic calcium concentration in different gravitational fields by the use of centrifuges, and 3) study calcium expression under simulated zero gravity by in situ instantaneous measurements on plants in free fall. This project will set the stage for further understanding the precise mechanisms by which various unique gravity stress stimuli generate distinct Ca2+ responses that result in distinct downstream physiologic responses.

Our repeated efforts with different moss strains created from the same batch of aequorin transformation using several detection systems failed to yield positive response.

description: The evaluation of sex differences in the time course of physiologic responses and adaptations to the space environment is critical to ensuring the safety of crews as the world prepares for the first crewed spaceflights beyond low Earth orbit in 50 years and the first woman to step on the Moon. Microgravity during spaceflight damages musculoskeletal tissues, but the understanding of sex differences in musculoskeletal atrophy during spaceflight is incomplete. Maintaining musculoskeletal health during long-duration spaceflight is crucial for ensuring astronauts are physically ready for exploration class missions and mission success upon return to partial weightbearing activity. Due to the known links between sex and musculoskeletal health, it is critical to get a better understanding of “how” and “why” bone microarchitectural and material property changes occur over a mission duration and if that change occurs differently in males and females. Finite element (FE) modeling protocols and computational models have been developed to better identify how bone strength is compromised during reduced weight-bearing and other challenges. Preliminary data using FE modeling on female mice flow on Space Shuttle mission STS-135 indicated that proximal tibia bone density loss (-17%) underpredicted the attenuation in structural strength (-34%). These findings demonstrate a limitation in the current clinical assessments of bone health and fracture risk using dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), as well as the standard micro computed tomography (microCT) analysis for predicting bone health during spaceflight. The objective of the current proposal is to capitalize on samples from two completed projects that the team has already acquired through tissue sharing opportunities. The parent projects had male and/or female mice that underwent unloading (hindlimb unloading or spaceflight) for 14, 28, or 38 days (and appropriate controls). We will quantify bone cellular, microarchitecture, and strength changes using histology, microCT, computational FE modeling, and material property characterization. Successful completion of this project will provide foundational data for further mechanistic and translational studies examining sex differences in the musculoskeletal adaptation to spaceflight environmental stressors that will enable more specific countermeasure development.
research_impact: The work is significant to NASA’s goal for maximizing astronaut health during long-duration spaceflight. The proposed work will provide critical insight on how changes in bone microarchitecture and material properties during spaceflight contribute to overall bone strength, which are important factors for understanding and mitigating fracture risk. The proposed work will synergize with the development of novel imaging modalities to monitor bone health and countermeasure development, which will benefit astronauts and people on Earth.

description: The combined effects of space environmental stressors induce pathologies in multiple organ systems. Specifically, losses to the musculoskeletal system may be very dangerous for the health and performance of astronauts on extended duration missions on the Moon or arriving on Mars. A critical need remains to better understand the impact of radiation exposure, one of the key environmental stressors of deep space, on human and animal physiology to enable extended duration missions beyond low Earth orbit or setting up settlements on the Moon or Mars. There is a critical gap in knowledge surrounding the impact of the space radiation environment on skeletal health and on the progress of fetal skeletal development during pregnancy. The objective of the current proposal is to capitalize on a unique tissue-sharing opportunity to examine the combined effects of continuous radiation exposure and pregnancy on maternal and fetal skeletal physiology. We propose to assess maternal and fetal skeletal physiology through measurements of mineral and material properties, as well as assess changes in cellular dynamics of the maternal bone under the microscope. This study will be critical in assessing how a very harmful component of the space radiation environment impacts multiple aspects of skeletal health, including sex-specific differences and individual variation in the impact of the space environment on the functioning of the body.

description: POSTDOCTORAL FELLOWSHIP Astronauts who spend a long time in weightlessness typically lose bone and muscle mass -- which may be very dangerous for astronauts arriving on Mars. Hormonal contraceptive (HC) methods routinely used female astronauts, and women worldwide, to suppress ovarian function and menstrual cycling. Use of HC decreases natural estrogen and progesterone exposure and the positive influence of both hormones on bone health. There is a critical gap in knowledge surrounding long-acting, reversible contraceptive (LARC; progestin-only) use, an HC option chosen with increasing frequency, and bone geometry and cellular activity. There is no knowledge about the interaction of LARC use and microgravity on bone health. Specific Aim 1: Determine the dose dependent impact of an etonogestrel (ENG) LARC implant on ovarian function in intact, young adult female rats over 28 days of exposure. Specific Aim 2: Determine the combined effects of an ENG LARC implant and skeletal disuse (hindlimb unloading; HU) on bone health in intact, young adult, female rats.
research_impact: This project will have impact with the shift from short to long duration and exploration class missions and has the potential to shift clinical practice. In female astronauts of reproductive age, the impact of spaceflight on gonadal function is complicated by the use of hormonal contraception to suppress the menstrual cycle pre-flight and during flight. Ground based studies have failed to directly account for the impact of long term use of hormonal contraception on bone health. We want to facilitate the improvement of best practice by working to ensure that long term use of hormonal contraception methods does not impair health. This study will be the first to explore the impact of LARC use on bone health using an animal model of microgravity exposure and will use measures of bone geometry, strength, and cellular activity. The results of this study will be translatable to the astronaut corps as well as millions of women around the world who use hormonal contraception. Additionally, this project is the development of a novel model to assess the impact of hormonal contraceptive use on bone health and future fracture risk.

description: Exposure to space irradiation presents a significant risk to flight crews in the course of prolonged space exploration. One of the greatest concerns is a possibility of radiation-induced deterioration to central nervous system functions. The primary sources of radiation include Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) and Solar Particle Events (SPE). GCR consist of the high-energy charged nuclei of approximately 83% hydrogen, 13% helium, and 1% high mass (Z>2) and energy (HZE) particles, whereas SPE are composed of mostly energetic protons. GCR ions are able to penetrate several tens of centimeters of materials such as aluminum. As a consequence, practical levels of shielding materials will not fully absorb all space radiation, and there will be unavoidable exposures to be kept to a minimum. While previous studies have been devoted primarily to the effects of single source irradiation, there is an imperative need to utilize exposures to two or more sources to better simulate the occupational exposure that will be encountered by astronauts. Photobiomodulation (PBM) is a technique where red to near-infrared red (NIR) light (600 to 1100 nm) is exposed to neural tissues. Light in this range can be absorbed by mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (CCO), the crucial chromophore which mediates the effects of PBM in cells. PBM can affect neuronal function by affecting mitochondrial reduction/oxidation (redox) signaling. PBM has been demonstrated to improve cognitive function for PBM enhanced total antioxidant capacity in the hippocampus and improved cognition in a preclinical model of Alzheimer's dementia. One of the main mediators of antioxidant mechanisms is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD). Multiple studies demonstrate that PBM decreases oxidative stress in mitochondria through increased MnSOD activity but it does not alter the protein expression of this mitochondrially localized antioxidant enzyme. Sirtuin 3 (Sirt3), which is the major deacetylase in mammalian mitochondria, has been linked to post-translational enzymatic activation of several metabolic enzymes, including MnSOD via deacetlyation of critical lysine residues on its active site. In this study, we propose to determine the role of Sirt3 signaling as a major regulator of increased MnSOD activity during transcranial PBM.
research_impact: There is currently no therapy that can reverse the effect of radiation-induced cognitive dysfunction. Clinically, photobiomodulation (PBM) is being tested as a therapy for impaired cognition following traumatic brain injury, and a randomized double-blind trial is currently enrolling participants. PBM has also improved executive functioning in a small cohort of patients with Alzheimer's dementia. These promising results indicate that PBM could be a successful therapy for cognitive impairment. While we do not know how PBM mediates beneficial effects, current preclinical studies indicate that it modulates mitochondrial redox pathways. The goal of the NASA space radiation protection program is to permit humans to live and work safely in space with an acceptable level of risk. The overarching program goal is to provide safe and effective medical countermeasures to protect astronauts of both sexes against the delayed radiation effects of galactic cosmic rays solar particle events. The proposed work will contribute to this goal by providing data about the neurological response to mixed field and protracted irradiation.
task_progress: Campaign 19C 6 Month old Male Mice received received .5 Gy SIM GCR (simulated galactic cosmic radiation). PBM Delivered 3 days per week for 3 months followed by cognitive testing. Y-Maze During the Y-maze, the amount of time a mouse spends exploring the novel arm of the maze compared to the familiar arm in the testing phase is indicative of its ability to retain the spatial memory encoded during the familiarization session. Sham, Sham/PBM, and Radiation/PBM animals displayed normal spatial recognition by exploring the novel arm during the testing session for a significantly longer period of time than they did the start and familiar arms: Radiation only significantly impaired short term memory they failed to distinguish the novel and familiar arms, by exploring all arms for approximately equal time, indicating a deficit in spatial memory. This data suggest that PBM preserves Short term memory tested in the Y-maze. Morris Water Maze Cognitive Testing: Latency to Platform: The Morris water maze was used to determine if PBM treatment reverses cognitive deficits after SIM GCR. Swim velocity can influence latency to the target during training sessions. The repeated-measures ANOVA revealed there was no significant effect of radiation treatment on swim speed. Further, all treatment groups were able to locate the visible platform. Animals were trained 5 days to find the hidden platform prior to the Probe trial. There was a main effect of radiation on latency to target. There was also a main effect of time on latency to target. Multiple comparison analysis showed non-PBM treated mice that received radiation took significantly longer time to locate to the platform compared to Sham, Sham/PBM, and Radiation/PBM treated animals on day 4. Probe Trial: During the probe trial, Sham treated and Sham/PBM mice showed memory retention by spending more time in the target quadrant than any other quadrant. In contrast, Radiation treated animals with Radiation only, or Radiation/PBM, did not show spatial memory retention. Overall it appears that PBM Spares Short Term Memory but not Spatial Memory. Dissociation and Flow cytometry analysis: Brain cortices were dissected, and dissociated by enzymatic digestion using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit An objective of this project to determine if/how those various endpoints are affected by PBM. The experimental methods chosen to accomplish these goals provide a means by which the effects of GCR and Fractionated Protons can be quantified both in terms of behavioral performance as well as specific cellular endpoints that are associated with hippocampal dependent learning and memory. We used flow cytometry to measure changes in Astrocytes (ACSA-2), Neural Precursor Cells (PSA-NCAM), Microglia (CD11b) and Oligodendrocytes (O4). We found No Significant changes in any of our measures cell counts ACSA-2. Campaign 20 B 9 Month old Male Mice received .5 Gy SIM GCR. Mice are 3 months older due to the cancelation of 20A. There appears to be gender differences in cognitive impairment dependent upon the Behavioral test performed. In the Y maze, Males are impaired; however, Females demonstrate no response to the irradiation. In the Morris Water maze, Males have intact Spatial memory where as Females are Impaired. Brain Hemi sections have been stained for Golgi Analysis; the other halves have been prepared for Metabolomics and Proteomic Analysis.

description: The proposed project aims to test the hypothesis that Ionizing Radiation (IR), microgravity, and social isolation combine synergistically to trigger an oxidative stress response that alters immune homeostasis, brain structure and function, and neurobehavioral and cognitive performance. Specific Aims for this project are: (1) Determine dose-response curves for acute ‘Five-Ion GCR (galactic cosmic ray) Simulation’ exposure for immune, brain, and performance responses in crew age-matched adult male and female mice; (2) Determine effects of acute ‘Five-Ion GCR Simulation’ exposure singly and in combination with simulated microgravity and social isolation, on immune, brain, and performance responses in crew age-matched male and female mice mimicking deep space missions; and (3) Determine efficacy of the dietary antioxidant, Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN), a key intermediate in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) biosynthesis. The project relies on established and highly translatable ground-based mouse models and assays with IR exposures to be performed at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL). The experimental approach will provide definitive data on the timing and mechanisms involved in the oxidative stress response, immune, and brain changes, and ensuing functional (behavioral/cognitive) impairments expected during human transit to Mars. This project will identify potential immune biomarkers for, and mechanisms underlying, structural and functional changes in the immune and nervous systems leading to behavioral/cognitive performance deficits, and its potential application to develop effective countermeasures to mitigate negative health effects of long duration space habitation. This proposal addresses NASA’s efforts to rapidly advance the characterization of risks and identifying appropriate countermeasures in anticipation of future deep space missions. Ensuring crew health and performance during extended transits necessitates that sensorimotor and cognitive abilities remain strong to avoid potentially catastrophic health and safety outcomes. Further, despite historically low numbers of females astronauts, recent NASA Astronaut Corps class selections, comprised of 50% and 40% women as compared to men, signal the need to understand how sex differences affect physiological adaptation and health in the space environment. This integrative project, developed by a cross-disciplinary team highly experienced in spaceflight and radiation research, utilizes established space biosciences research protocols and variables, and time-honored, as well as modern, research methodologies. We will address major risks and associated gaps: (1) Risk of Acute (In-flight) and Late Central Nervous System Effects from Radiation (CNS), (2) Risk of Altered Sensorimotor/Vestibular Function Impacting Critical Mission Tasks (SM), and Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders that have been combined into the NASA CNS, BMed, and SM (CBS) Integrated Research Plan. Here we have adhered to primary goals set forth in Human Exploration Research Opportunities (HERO) Appendix A to determine how key features of the deep space environment may interact to increase risk to a crew by negatively impacting health and performance, and we have identifed and developed strategies to characterize and mitigate the potential risks via countermeasures.
research_impact: This project is testing the overall hypothesis that Ionizing Radiation (IR), microgravity and social isolation combine synergistically to trigger an oxidative stress response that alters immune homeostasis, brain structure and function, and neurobehavioral and cognitive performance. In this project, we assessed sexually dimorphic immune and endocrine responses to cosmic ionizing radiation, hindlimb unloading, and social isolation. Based on foreseen immune and endocrine deficits, the central nervous system most likely plays a significant role in crosstalk regulation, which requires further studies. Additionally, the involvement of sex hormones on adrenal and immune function adds an additional layer of complexity during integrative crosstalk, which could be negatively affected by space irradiation based on ovarian health assessment. Generally, female mice produced rapid selective immune responses and resolve compared to male mice in blood, along with contributing adrenal hormone influence. In short, this study identified notable immune and endocrine integrative pathways that are sexually dimorphic. Advances in this research can direct personalized medicine and pharmaceutical approaches for future exploration and commercial missions.
task_progress: Over the course of this project, extensive progress was made on the first two project aims, yielding six publications, multiple datasets, and multiple abstracts to date focused on assessing combined stressors related to spaceflight. Specifically, we assessed the acute Galactic Cosmic Ray simulation (GCRsim) dose-response and combinatorial effects with other spaceflight stressors (isolation, simulated weightlessness) on adult male and female mice. Data were collected on neural, behavioral, cardiac, reproductive, and immune outcomes at varying timepoints following the experiment period to characterize acute, intermediate, or late effects from simulated spaceflight stressors.
